(a) Section 18(b) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(b)) is amended—

        (1) 
by inserting “(1)” after the subsection designation;
 
        (2) 
by redesignating paragraph (11 through paragraph (4) as subparagraph (A) through subparagraph (D), respectively; and
 
        (3) 
by adding at the end thereof the following new paragraph:

“(2)(A) Prior to the publication of any notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to paragraph (1)(A), the Commission snail publish an advance notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register. Such advance notice shall—
“(i) contain a brief description of the area of inquiry under consideration, the objectives which the Commission seeks to achieve, and possible regulatory alternatives under consideration by the Commission; and
“(ii) invite the response of interested parties with respect to such proposed rulemaking, including any suggestions or alternative methods for achieving such objectives.

“(B) The Commission shall submit such advance notice of proposed rulemaking to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and to the Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce of the House of Representatives. The Commission may use such additional mechanisms as the Commission considers useful to obtain suggestions regarding the content of the area of inquiry before the publication of a general notice of proposed rulemaking under paragraph (1)(A).


“(C) The Commission shall, 30 days before the publication of a notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to paragraph (1)(A), submit such notice to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation of the Senate and to the Committee on Interstate and Foreign Commerce of the House of Representatives.”.

  
    (b)
        (1) Section 18(c) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(c)) is amended by striking out “subsection (b)(3)” and inserting in lieu thereof “subsection (b)(1)(C)”. 
        (2) 
Section 18(e)(5)(C) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. 57a(e)(5)(C)) is amended by striking out “subsection (b)(4)” and inserting in lieu thereof “subsection (b)(1)(D)”.

fable.w: The section requires the FTC to publish an advance notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register that invites responses from interested parties, which brings people outside the federal government into the rulemaking decision. The tempting opposite reading is that the section is only about submitting notices to Senate and House committees, which stays inside the federal government and would be a "No". That reading fails because the invitation to interested parties is a separate requirement that crosses the federal boundary.
fable.s: invite the response of interested parties with respect to such proposed rulemaking, including any suggestions or alternative methods for achieving such objectives

opus.w: The section requires the FTC to publish an advance notice of proposed rulemaking in the Federal Register and to invite responses from interested parties before it proposes a rule. That is a required rulemaking and comment process involving people outside the federal government. Sending the notices to congressional committees would not count on its own, because Congress is inside the federal government. However, it does not cancel out the required outreach to the public.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires the Commission to publish an advance notice of proposed rulemaking that explicitly invites responses from 'interested parties,' which are entities outside the federal government. This constitutes a public comment period or consultation with the public before a federal decision (rulemaking) is finalized. The requirement to submit notices to Congress is internal and does not override the external participation mandate.
qwen_chat.s: invite the response of interested parties with respect to such proposed rulemaking, including any suggestions or alternative methods for achieving such objectives.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue "No" because the section also requires submitting notices to Congressional committees, and Congress is inside the federal government. However, the definition explicitly states that participation involves consulting with people *outside* the government, and the section clearly mandates inviting responses from "interested parties" (the general public/companies) via an advance notice of proposed rulemaking. The presence of internal reporting requirements does not negate the external participation requirement.
